I thought about this after I was ready to post this and I used some short hand that us gamers know very well, but someone who is new to the scene might not. So I used a term (explanation of term) set up for the first use. I think I got it all. To the new people, hi! welcome! to the rest of you, please read.

eSports need regulation in areas outside of personality. Baseball, for example, a player is part of a team which is apart of a brand. eSports players are a brand in and of their own. They are in a unique position where they are able to brand themselves and make themselves seem more marketable and thereby more valuable to have. Additionally the culture surrounding eSports is different than regular sports and ignoring that is going to set dangerous and detrimental precedent. We appreciate the gg (good game) after good matches and wishing the opposing team gl hf (good luck, have fun) in the next round when you lose is proper sportsmanship, the interviews afterwards is where some trash talking, #rekt commentary comes out.

Players, by and large from what I've been able to see, understand that acting in an irate manner might get you attention quickly. However it will destroy your brand with the most famous example I can think of is IdrA. From personal experience; I watched his matches and saw how quickly the bm (bad manners) flows from him outside of the professional scene. In ladder matches I see him attacking the player both with units and with words. I watched him give interviews after wins and losses in tournaments and saw the game be respectful but him being dismissive. I understand that part of him. The ladder antics, however, turned me off from him. While he was apparently trying to build his brand as the 'bad boy' of gaming, all he managed to do was turn this viewer off from his games. I stopped watching anything with him in it and just ignored him.

eSports players have fellow gamers around to judge their actions. A committee might not represent us down the road and consider an after the game jab at an opponent, like "he got lucky", to be bm and as such worthy of a fine as you are putting down their skill level. Where as players of the game know that even with gosu senses you know checking that area for anything isn't done and it was literally a misclick or a misrally of a unit that just managed to catch the enemy moving and you saw it and they didn't meaning you could prepare, etc.

The regulations that need to be taken care of are drugs. Specifically anything than boosts alertness, attentiveness, and awareness. For example Adderall testing SHOULD be done. If two players of equal skill go head to head late in the day, the one on Adderall has an advantage, well anyone taking an amphetamine has an advantage. In baseball amphetamines are just as illegal as steroids, for eSports determining the drugs to ban should be the focus over behavioral regulation.

In short controlling behaviors should be as minimal as possible while drug testing should be a major focus in the early days. As a final though the issue about 'match fixing' is a problem. If a team wants to seed the rankings by losing matches intentionally by not playing well to give themselves an easier time and give their opponents a harder time (like a 1st seed team tossing games to drop to 4th or 5th and forcing everyone else up ranks) it might be see as a fix. That is something that might need watching and very fluid rules.
